html:
The Kadiwéu are an Indigenous people of Mato Grosso do Sul, in western Brazil, near the Paraguay River and the Pantanal wetlands. They are the last surviving group of the Mbayá, a branch of the Guaykuruan-speaking peoples of the Chaco.

The Mbayá took up horses from the Spanish in the 1600s and became feared mounted raiders, ruling over farming neighbours such as the Terena, who paid them in crops. They are still known for their riding.

In the Paraguayan War of 1864 to 1870 the Kadiwéu fought for Brazil, and they say the land they hold today was their reward. They are also famous for their women's painting: fine geometric designs drawn on faces, bodies and pottery. The anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss studied these designs in the 1930s and wrote about them in Tristes Tropiques.
